contributes.instructions: The css-author plugin contributes two gates, which `lint` runs over the project's pages, their findings blocking save the few they mark advisory: the static lint (facts from a page's markup and stylesheets — a length with no unit, a restated initial value, a font face nothing names, a class no rule names, a stray `;` that makes the browser drop the rule after it — and what matching the page decides: a rule that matches nothing, a declaration another already makes, a container query no ancestor can answer) and the necessity lint (each declaration removed in the rendered page and restored; one that changes no element's geometry or computed style at the viewport's width nor at a sweep of other widths is dead). Their findings name an element by its unique selector, and a rule by its selector as written and the stylesheet it is written in — the project file, or the page's `<style>` block — which is the one to edit; a remote stylesheet's rules are never a finding's subject. Treat their findings as the Core tools section says. A viewport is authored as a draft the user watches take shape: draft_open is the FIRST call of the task — the frame, the title and the html › body skeleton with its page background (never a page without one), sent before knowledge_bundle, before any reading, before planning — then knowledge_bundle {query: <the task in a few words>} ONCE (it returns the format rules with the example nearest the task), then one visual group per draft_append as each is written — its markup and the css it needs, a rule the group shares sent with it — and once it is complete, the page is written into the project's files as the dream-author prompt says, and linted there. The layout procedures (which formatting context, whether a declaration is needed at all, where in the cascade it goes) are this plugin's: read them once per task with knowledge_read {path: "mrbavio.css-author/procedures.md"} (or the `procedures` resource) and judge every declaration by them. The author → write → lint → fix workflow is Daydream's own dream-author prompt: start every document task from it.
